CITATION:
R. v. Katsnelson, 2010 ONSC 2246

COURT FILE NO.:

0039/09

DATE:
20100414

ONTARIO

SUPERIOR COURT OF JUSTICE

B E T W E E N:

)

)

HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN

)

Andrew Locke and Melissa Montemurro for the Crown

)

DANIEL KATSNELSON

Mary Cremer for Daniel Katsnelson

)

)

Heard
: January 18 and March 26, 2010

MacDonnell, J:

[
1
]

On January 18, 2010, Daniel Katsnelson appeared before this court and
was arraigned on an indictment containing the following two counts:

(
1)
Daniel Katsnelson stands…charged that he, on or about the 7
th
day of
September in the year 2007, in the City of Toronto, in the Toronto Region, did
in committing a sexual assault on C.C., wound the said C.C., thereby committing
an aggravated sexual assault, contrary to
s. 273(1)
of the
Criminal Code
.

***

(3) Daniel
Katsnelson stands further charged that he, on or about the 7
th
day
of September in the year 2007, in the City of Toronto, in the Toronto Region,
did commit a sexual assault on B.M., contrary to
s. 271
of the
Criminal Code
.

[
2
]

With respect to Count 1, Mr. Katsnelson pleaded not guilty to the
offence charged but guilty to the included offence of sexual assault causing
bodily harm. He pleaded guilty as charged to Count 3. The proceedings were then
adjourned to March 26, 2010 for a sentencing hearing. At the conclusion of that
hearing, Mr. Katsnelson was remanded in custody to today for the imposition of
sentence.

I. The Facts

(a) The Circumstances of the Offences

[
3
]

The circumstances surrounding the commission of the offences are set
forth in an agreed statement of facts, which reveals the following.

[
4
]

Mr. Katsnelson graduated from York University in 2006. At the time of
the offences, in September, 2007, he was 25 years of age and he was working
full-time for a travel insurance company.

[
5
]

On the evening of September 6, 2007, Mr. Katsnelson and his long-time
friend Justin Connort, who was also 25 years of age, were “partying” near the
campus of York University. Both were consuming alcohol.

[
6
]

In the early morning hours of September 7, Mr. Katsnelson and Mr.
Connort ended up on the York University campus inside the Vanier residence.
They did not have permission to be within those premises. They gained entry by
pretending that they were helping an intoxicated resident to his room. In fact,
they were looking to engage in sexual activity. They began to walk from floor
to floor, trying the doors of the residence rooms. They were able to determine
which rooms were occupied by female students because it was “Frosh Week” at the
university and the names of the occupants were displayed on the doors.

[
7
]

C.C. was a 17-year-old first year York University student who was living
on the seventh floor of the Vanier residence. At around 2:45 a.m. she was
awakened by the sound of her door opening, and she observed Mr. Katsnelson and Mr.
Connort entering her room. Both men were complete strangers to her. They
attempted to engage her in conversation, asking her, among other things, “Do
you have a boyfriend?”, and “Do you want to get lucky with a couple of Jewish
guys?” Mr. Katsnelson asked her if he could lie down beside her. She said no,
but he did so anyway. He lay on the bed, by the wall, facing C.C.’s back.
Connort was on the other side of the bed, kneeling on the floor, close to
C.C.’s face. The room was dark.

[
8
]

Mr. Katsnelson stroked C.C.’s back and side, and then began to remove
her pajama bottoms while Connort was kissing her on the face and neck. Mr.
Katsnelson removed his own pants. C.C. struggled and began to cry. Katsnelson
proceeded to have vaginal intercourse with her from behind, to the point of
ejaculation.

[
9
]

Mr. Katsnelson then got off of the bed, crossed the room and lay down on
C.C.’s roommate’s bed. Meanwhile, Justin Connort continued to sexually assault
C.C. He digitally penetrated her, but he did not have sexual intercourse with
her. Mr. Katsnelson used his cell phone to take pictures of Connort assaulting
C.C. Katsnelson then lay down beside her again. He attempted to open her legs
and to have sexual intercourse a second time. She resisted. Mr. Katsnelson then
got up and put his pants on. Either Katsnelson or Connort said “Fuck this,
let’s get out of here”, and they left the room.

[
10
]

For
about a week following this ordeal C.C. experienced bleeding from her vagina.

[
11
]

Unfortunately,
when Katsnelson and Connort left C.C.’s room they were not finished. At around
3:00 a.m., Y.W., a 19-year-old first-year student living on the fourth floor of
the Vanier residence woke up to find a male entering her room. She sat up and
looked at him, and he left. She went back to sleep. At around 3:50 a.m., a
second male opened her door and entered her room. She felt something rub
against her, and she sat up and asked the male what he was doing. He told her
that he was in a hurry and that he wanted to borrow a bottle of water. She gave
him a bottle and told him to leave, and he did. Katsnelson and Connort were the
two men who had entered Y.W.’s room. Both were complete strangers to her.

[
12
]

At
around 3:45 a.m., Katsnelson and Connort entered another fourth floor room,
where S.R., an 18-year-old first-year student, was sleeping. One of the men sat
on S.R.’s bed. They engaged her in a short conversation and then left.  At
around 4:00 a.m., they entered the third-floor room of C.H., an 18-year-old
first-year exchange student. She woke up when they entered. One of them told
C.H. that he had never made out with a black girl and asked her if he could
make out with her. She said no. He repeated the request and again she said no.
The men then left.

[
13
]

At
about 4:40 a.m., Katsnelson and Connort entered the 13
th
floor room
of B.M., another 18-year-old first-year student. B.M. awoke when the men
entered. The room was dark. Katsnelson walked over to B.M. while Justin Connort
sat on her roommate’s bed. Katsnelson asked if he could sit down. B.M.
mistakenly thought that she knew him and so she said “sure”. He lay down beside
her and began fondling her, touching her breasts and putting his hand inside
her underwear. He then removed her pajama bottoms and underwear, pulled off his
own pants, and, against her will and without her consent, had sexual
intercourse with her.

[
14
]

Mr.
Katsnelson did not use a condom while having sexual intercourse with either
C.C. or B.M.

(b) The Investigation and Prosecution

[
15
]

In
the course of the subsequent police investigation, forensic evidence
identifying Katsnelson and Connort as the intruders was obtained. Mr.
Katsnelson’s semen was found on both C.C.’s bed sheet and her underwear. His
semen was also found on a vaginal swab obtained from B.M. Justin Connort’s fingerprints
were found in C.C.’s room and S.R.’s room, and the DNA of both men was found on
a water bottle in B.M.’s room.

[
16
]

In
due course, both men were arrested. A preliminary inquiry was held in December
2008. Both C.C. and B.M. testified and were cross-examined. At the conclusion
of the preliminary inquiry, Connort pleaded guilty to a single count of sexual
assault, which pertained to his digital penetration of C.C. He was sentenced to
three years in the penitentiary. Mr. Katsnelson was committed to stand trial in
the Superior Court.

[
17
]

In
January, 2010, on the eve of trial in the Superior Court, Mr. Katsnelson’s
counsel advised the Crown Attorney’s Office that Mr. Katsnelson intended to
plead guilty.

(c) The Impact of the Offences on the Victims

[
18
]

Victim
impact statements were prepared by C.C. and her mother as well as by B.M and
S.R.

[
19
]

In
the course of her statement, C.C. related the following:

September
7, 2007 has changed my life forever and I would like to tell you how. I was
taken to Women Hospital for an examination at which time they advised me to
take medication for STDs, AIDS and the morning after pill. I had to take the
AIDS medication for 3 months which made me sick to my stomach and made me feel
tired & drained all the time which was hard while I was trying to study at
University. The thought of not knowing whether I had any of these diseases
really weighed on my mind as well as my family’s – all the what ifs. I had to
be tested until 1 year after the incident to make sure there were no signs of
disease…

***

I am afraid of the
dark and always sleep with the TV or a night light. I never leave the door
unlocked anymore for anything whether it be day or night.

[
20
]

C.C.
stated that a year after the incident she was still having constant nightmares
and that she was taking medication. She eventually began seeing a psychologist.
She stated that she finds it almost impossible to trust persons of the opposite
sex. She said that rape is like a tattoo: “it may fade away with time but it
will never be gone.” She concluded:

After 2½ years I
still suffer from panic and anxiety attacks, nightmares, flashbacks and I’m
still afraid of the dark. I am continually in therapy, and I can’t concentrate
or stay focused on anything and I’m not doing well in school. I have switched
to another college but I am still haunted by what happened to me daily.

This sexual assault
has had a profound effect on my life which I will never forget… I have been
given a life sentence to deal with through no fault of my own. My hopes and
dreams of becoming a dancer have been taken away from me and I’m not sure if I
will ever be truly happy again.

[
21
]

The
victim impact statement of C.C.’s mother sets forth the profound impact that
the offence has had on their family. She stated that “it is almost impossible
to put into words the sickness that I feel every time I think about that
night…” She had to go on short-term disability and she continues to suffer from
panic and anxiety attacks, bouts of depression and nightmares. C.C.’s father
had to leave his job as a seaman because of the strain that his wife and daughter
were suffering.

[
22
]

In
her victim impact statement, B.M. stated:

In the last three
years I have spent every day pushing the thoughts of what happened to me out of
my head. But no matter how much I try it always comes back up. Sometimes in
dreams, conversation, events, the news… I think about it every day without fail…
It has effected every part of my life putting strain on my family, friends,
school work, relationships, health and so much more. What happened to me that
night is never far from my mind and I’m sure now that I will never be the same.
I lost a big part of myself that night and in the days that followed. I’ve lost
a trust that I used to have in people. I’ve lost the sense of independence. I
no longer trust in strangers and always keep people at a distance. I no longer
feel safe when I’m alone, or going out at night… More than anything else I lost
something that I can never get back, I lost my virginity which left me to feel
like I was just damaged goods. I know I’ll learn to trust again and some of the
memories will fade over the years but I am no longer the girl that I once was
and I will never be that person again. I can’t begin even to tell you how much
this event changed my life, there just aren’t words for it.

[
23
]

With
respect to the physical impact of the incident, B.M. stated:

For the most part
the physical impact is long past… The first pain I endured was in the first 24
hrs or so after the rape, like I already mentioned at this point I was still a
virgin and I experienced physical pain and discomfort both during the rape and
in the day following. Most of the physical impact following the first 24 hrs of
the attack had to do with the things I had to do and take in order to protect
myself. Because I was not given the sexual background of my attackers I had to
take all the precautions necessary in order to protect myself. I took several
tests and drugs to prevent pregnancy and sexually transmitted diseases… I had
to take preventative HIV drugs for approximately a month… While on these drugs
I found myself constantly nauseous and regularly vomiting, fatigued and had a
great loss of appetite and weight loss. The only physical aspect that still
plagues me is that of sleep deprivation. After the attack I became dependent on
sleeping pills… I’m no longer dependent on them because I have developed other
strategies to replace them but there are still nights that nothing other than a
sleeping pill will allow me to stop thinking and just sleep.

[
24
]

B.M.
has been and continues to be under professional counseling.

(d) The Circumstances of the Offender

[
25
]

Mr.
Katsnelson was 25 years of age at the time of the offences. He is now 27 years
old. He has no prior criminal record. He was raised by his mother and
stepfather in a normal, happy, supportive middle-class environment. He is close
to both parents. He has a number of close friends who speak well of him. He
graduated from high school in 2001, and then attended York University,
graduating in 2006 with a Bachelor of Arts degree in Business and Society.

[
26
]

While
attending university, Mr. Katsnelson was employed as a service provider of
after-school and lunch time special-interest programs, providing sports-based
and science-based activities for a local school board. He eventually
established his own company to provide similar programs to schools in York
Region. In the past, he has also worked as a counselor at children’s day and
overnight camps, both in Canada in the United States and at one point he had
hoped to operate his own summer camp.

[
27
]

Following
his graduation from York University, Mr. Katsnelson worked for a travel
insurance brokerage company. He lost that job when he was arrested for the
present offences. Since September 2007, when he was released on a strict house-arrest
bail order, he has succeeded in getting an “environmental loyalty program” up
and running. The aim of the program is to bring together environmentally
responsible businesses and environmentally conscious consumers. The company he
founded for this purpose has entered into a contract with the City of Toronto.

[
28
]

The author
of the Presentence Report summed up her assessment of Mr. Katsnelson as follows:

While [Mr.
Katsnelson] notes he deserves to be incarcerated, he says he will forever try
to atone for what he did. He adds he wants to be able to give back to society,
and that if there was any way he could help or do something beneficial for the
victim, he would do so, adding he hopes she can move on with her life and try
to find joy and happiness.

He states he hopes
someday the victim will be able to take away something positive from this, as
he has, and when asked by the writer what that might be, he suggested that now
maybe she will know to keep her doors locked, while adding that the offence
would have been devastating to her.

He
suggests that “I believe this happened because I was heading down a very
destructive path”, and that he has now changed as a result of his behaviour. He
does not believe he requires any counseling. “I made my bed and I will lie in
it”, he says, noting “it is not who I am – I am not violent…was a combination
of a lot of bad things”.

***

Many sources
contacted for the purpose of preparing this report concur the subject’s
behaviour was out of character, and that, while he would party, drink and at
times did not act responsibly or exercise a mature attitude toward women, he
was generally a law-abiding and respectful member of society.

Although the subject
indicates he has some understanding of the impact of his behaviour on the
victims, the writer has some concerns regarding his possible lack of insight
with regard to the offences for which he currently stands before the Court.

(e)
Mr. Katsnelson’s Statement to the Court

[
29
]

At
the conclusion of the sentencing proceedings on March 26, 2010, Mr. Katsnelson read
a statement to the court pursuant to
s. 726
of the
Criminal Code
. In
that statement, he stated, in part, as follows:

I’m so sorry to the
victims, their families, York University and everyone else affected by my
actions. I made a terrible mistake and I’m so ashamed the victims and their
families have to live with this for the rest of their lives. I’m so sorry that
my actions were written into your lives like this. I am ashamed to [have]
brought into question the safety of our schools. I am not a violent person. I
made a terrible mistake, a mistake that would serve as a constant reminder of
something that I would never let happen again. I understand that I’m going to
prison. And once allowed out I’ll begin to repay my debt to society by ensuring
that there will never be another victim… Over the past two-and-a-half years on
bail I have felt terrible pain, shame, regret and remorse…

I will forever
regret and never forget my actions. I can’t believe how many people’s lives
were affected by this. I have learned a great deal and will continue to do so
each passing day and I can assure you I will never do anything like this again.
I sincerely hope that everyone, especially the victims, will get some closure.
I’m so sorry. Please forgive me.

(f) The Positions of the Parties

[
30
]

On
behalf of the Crown, Mr. Locke submitted that the global sentence imposed on
Mr. Katsnelson for the two offences to which he has pleaded guilty should be a
term of imprisonment of not less than ten years. The Crown also seeks an order
under
s. 109
of the
Criminal Code
, a DNA order and an order requiring Mr.
Katsnelson to comply with the
Sex Offender Information Registration Act

(“
SOIRA
”).

[
31
]

On
behalf of Mr. Katsnelson, Ms Cremer submitted that the appropriate total sentence
in this case is a term of imprisonment of between three and five years. She does
not oppose any of the ancillary orders sought by the Crown.

II. Analysis

(a) The Relevant Statutory Provisions

[
32
]

Section
718
of the
Criminal Code
provides, in part, that the fundamental purpose
of sentencing “is to contribute… to respect for the law and the maintenance of
a just, peaceful and safe society by imposing just sanctions that have one or
more of [six] objectives.” Those objectives include the denunciation of
unlawful conduct, deterrence of the offender and others who might be similarly
tempted, separation of the offender from society where necessary, rehabilitation,
and the promotion of a sense of responsibility in the offender. Whatever
sanction is imposed “must be proportionate to the gravity of the offence and
the degree of responsibility of the offender.”
[1]

Further, a court that imposes a sentence “shall also take into consideration”
the principles, among others, that “a sentence should be similar to sentences
imposed on similar offenders for similar offences committed in similar
circumstances”
[2]
,
and that “where consecutive sentences are imposed, the combined sentence should
not be unduly long or harsh”.
[3]

[
33
]

Ordinarily, a sentencing court has discretion to determine which
sentencing objectives should be considered paramount in all of the
circumstances of the case. With respect to the count of sexual assault causing
bodily harm to C.C., however, that discretion is not available. At the time of
the offence, C.C. was under the age of eighteen years, and
s. 718.01
of the
Criminal
Code
provides that in imposing sentence for an offence involving the abuse
of a person under the age of eighteen years, a sentencing court “shall give
primary consideration to the objectives of denunciation and deterrence of such
conduct”. Further, s. 718.2(a), which provides that the quantum of
sentence should be increased or reduced to reflect the presence of aggravating
or mitigating circumstances, specifically provides that “evidence that the
offender, in committing the offence, abused a person under the age of eighteen
years…shall be deemed to be [an] aggravating [circumstance]”.
[4]

(b) Sentencing Precedents

[
34
]

The principle
that “a sentence should be similar to sentences imposed on
similar offenders for similar offences committed in similar circumstances”
inevitably draws a sentencing court to a consideration of sentencing precedents.
The parties have referred to 19 cases in an effort to
support their conflicting positions as the appropriate range for Mr.
Katsnelson’s conduct:
R. v. C.A.M
.,
1996 CanLII 230 (SCC)
, [1996] 1 S.C.R. 500;
R. v. Myers
,

[2000] O.J. No. 1787 (Ont. S.C.)
, affirmed
[2002] O.J. No. 965 (C.A.)
;
R. v.
Smith
,
[2001] O.J. No. 4512 (Ont. C.J.)
, affirmed
[2002] O.J. No. 1912
);
R.
v. Crick
, [1991] Ont. D. Crim. Sent. 7517-02 (Ont. Ct. Gen. Div.);
R. v.
M.A
.,
[1996] O.J. No. 2899 (Ont. S.C.)
; R
. v. Delaney
,
[2003] O.J.
No. 3151 (Ont. C.J.)
;
R. v. Clement
,

[1991] B.C.J. No. 2713 (C.A.)
;
R. v. Staley
,
[1994]
B.C.J. No. 2339 (C.A.)
;
R. v. R.D.H
.,
[1999] B.C.J. No. 782 (C.A.)
;
R.
v. J.R.
,
2006 CanLII 40236 (ON SC)
, [2006] O.J. No. 4777 (Ont. S.C.);
R. v. Perkins
,
[2006]
O.J. No. 428 (Ont. S.C.)
;
R. v. Quashie
,
2005 CanLII 23208 (ON CA)
, [2005] O.J. No. 2694 (C.A.);
R.
v. Ramcharitar
,
[2005] O.J. No. 1528 (Ont. S.C.)
;
R. v. Bell
,
[2004]
O.J. No. 4046 (Ont. S.C.)
;
R. v. Balcolm
,
[2003] O.J. No. 3227 (Ont.
S.C.)
;
R. v. Bell
,
[2000] O.J. No. 4565 (C.A.)
;
R. v. Jamieson
,

[1997] O.J. No. 1111 (C.A.)
;
R. v. R.B
.,
[1998] O.J. No. 5859 (Ont. Ct.
Gen. Div.)
; R
. v. Gendreau
,
[1995] A.J. No. 1123 (C.A.)

[
35
]

The exercise of reviewing those cases is helpful, but one must be cautious
in attempting to fit the circumstances of one case into the factual footprint
of another. Sentencing remains pre-eminently a case-specific exercise. In
R. v. L.M.
,
2008 SCC 31
, at
paragraph
36
, LeBel J. stated:

Owing to the very
nature of an individualized sentencing process, sentences imposed for offences
of the same type will not always be identical. The principle of parity
does not preclude disparity
where warranted by the circumstances
,
because of the principle of proportionality.  As this Court
noted in
M. (C.A.)
,
at para.
92
, ‘there is no such thing as a uniform sentence for a
particular crime’. [emphasis in the original]

[
36
]

While
sexual assaults that involve rape can only be characterized as serious, the
wide range of sentences imposed for such offences reflects the diversity of the
circumstances in which the offence can be committed and the great variety of
offenders who may commit it. Accordingly, it is important to carefully consider
the particular circumstances of both the offence and the offender in attempting
to fashion a fit sentence.

(c) The Offender’s Rehabilitative Prospects

[
37
]

No
one, including Mr. Katsnelson, minimizes the seriousness of the offences. In
focusing on the gravity of what Mr. Katsnelson did, however, one must not lose
sight of the fact that he is more than his conduct on September 7, 2007, that
he is an individual with strengths, weaknesses and potential, and that he will
be returned to the community at the end of his term of imprisonment. While his rehabilitation
is not the paramount sentencing concern in this case, neither is it irrelevant.

[
38
]

The
incongruity between Mr. Katsnelson’s previous good character and the offences
he committed on September 7, 2007 is startling. He had no prior involvement
with the criminal justice system. Over the years, he had demonstrated himself
to be responsible, industrious, a self-starter, someone who could be expected
to make a positive contribution to the community. He was gainfully employed at
the time of the offences. After being arrested and losing his job, he threw himself
into the creation of another company, and but for the uncertainty created by
his present jeopardy, that company would seem to have potential for success.

[
39
]

Mr.
Katsnelson has expressed remorse, both in his statement to the court at the end
of the sentencing proceedings and in the Presentence Report. The Crown placed
emphasis on one particular statement made by Mr. Katsnelson to the author of
the Report in which, in response to a question as to what the victims of the
offences might take from what had happened to them, he stated they might now
know to keep their doors locked. Obviously this was not an insightful comment,
but in fairness it was immediately followed with a statement recognizing that
the offences were devastating for the victims.

[
40
]

None
of this, of course, diminishes the need to impose a sentence aimed squarely at
denouncing his conduct and at sending a clear warning to others, but there is
no reason to think that a sentence of imprisonment in either of the ranges proposed
by the parties would be insufficient to deter him from future misconduct.

(d) The Mitigating Effect of a Guilty Plea

[
41
]

Generally
speaking, a plea of guilty is a mitigating circumstance in the determination of
sentence, although the extent to which it will ameliorate the penalty that
would otherwise have been imposed will vary from case to case.

[
42
]

Where
the ability of the Crown to prove guilt beyond a reasonable doubt is a live
issue, surrendering the right to put the Crown to the proof of its case may be
regarded as a true sign of remorse. A plea of guilty in those circumstances may
be given greater weight than where the offender “was caught
red-handed ...had no defence to the charges and a trial would simply have
postponed the inevitable”:
R.
v. Daya
,
2007 ONCA 693
, at paragraph
15
; cf.
R. v. Santos

(1993), 67 O.A.C. 270 (C.A.)
. In my view, this case is one in which Mr.
Katsnelson’s conviction was all but inevitable. The forensic evidence identifying
him as the person who raped both C.C. and B.M. was formidable, and Justin
Connort was ready to testify against him.

[
43
]

I
acknowledge that because Mr. Katsnelson pleaded guilty the victims were spared
the trauma of again setting out in a public courtroom the intimate details of
what Mr. Katsnelson did to them. There is an important public interest in
encouraging offenders to plead guilty in sexual assault cases, and an effective
mechanism for providing that encouragement is to respond to a plea of guilty with
a reduction in the penalty that the offender would otherwise have received:
R.
v. R. W. E.
,

2007 ONCA 461
, 221 C.C.C. (3d) 244, at paragraph

40
. However, the credit that Mr. Katsnelson should receive for his plea of
guilty is attenuated by its timing. As I have said, a full preliminary inquiry
was held at which both victims testified and were cross-examined. Further, because
Mr. Katsnelson waited until the eve of trial before making the decision to
plead guilty, the victims were required to once again go through the difficult
process of preparing themselves to testify.

(e) Parity in Sentencing

[
44
]

While
not arguing that her client should receive the same sentence as that imposed on
Justin Connort, Ms. Cremer submitted that to impose a sentence in the range
urged by the Crown would offend the principle of parity in sentencing.

[
45
]

The principle set forth in
s. 718.2
(b) of the
Criminal
Code
that "a sentence should be similar to sentences imposed on
similar offenders for similar offences committed in similar circumstances"
requires a consideration not only of sentences imposed in unrelated but
analogous cases but also of the sentence imposed on any other person involved
in the offences for which the offender is to be sentenced. This does not mean
that everyone involved in an offence, regardless of their individual roles,
backgrounds and circumstances, should receive the same punishment. In
R.
v. Issa

(1992), 57 O.A.C. 253, at page 255,
the Court of Appeal explained
the principle as follows:

So long as sentencing
remains an individual process, there may be sentences meted out to offenders
for participation in the same offence which are justifiably disparate. I think
that Clayton Ruby's statement in
Sentencing
(3d ed, 1987), at p. 29, is
correct, that the rule against unreasonable disparity in sentencing 'does not
require equal sentences, but only understandable sentences, when examined
together'.

[
46
]

It
is true that for sentencing purposes there are similarities between the
circumstances of Justin Connort and those of Mr. Katsnelson. They were the same
age, they appear to have similar backgrounds, and neither of them had a prior
criminal record. Further, in entering the Vanier residence that morning, they
were engaged in a joint enterprise.

[
47
]

However,
there are also important differences between the situation that was presented
to the judge who sentenced Connort and the situation that this court is faced
with today. Connort pleaded guilty and was sentenced for
one
offence – a
sexual assault on C.C. Mr. Katsnelson is to be sentenced for two offences, a
charge of sexual assault causing bodily harm in relation to C.C. and a sexual
assault on B.M. While Connort’s conduct in relation to C.C. was reprehensible
and deserving of significant punishment, and while he was in law a party to
what Mr. Katsnelson did to C.C., his conduct did not include sexual
intercourse. Mr. Katsnelson, on the other hand, vaginally raped both C.C. and
B.M., and on neither occasion did he use a condom.

[
48
]

Further,
Connort pleaded guilty immediately at the conclusion of the preliminary
inquiry. Mr. Katsnelson did not plead guilty until the day on which his trial
was to begin in the Superior Court, and he did not notify the Crown of his
intention to plead guilty until a matter of days prior to that.

[
49
]

In the
circumstances, what would offend the principle of parity would be to fail to
impose a sentence on Mr. Katsnelson that was markedly different from the
sentence that Justin Connort received. What Connort did was seriously wrong, as
the three-year penitentiary sentence he received indicates, but his role within
the common factual matrix of this case is readily distinguishable from that of
Mr. Katsnelson.

(f) The Need to Denounce and Deter

[
50
]

As I mentioned earlier,
s. 718.01
of the
Criminal Code

provides that in imposing sentence for an offence involving the abuse of a
person under the age of eighteen years, a sentencing court “shall give primary
consideration to the objectives of denunciation and deterrence of such conduct.”
Because C.C. was under the age of 18 years at the time of the incident, that
statutory direction applies to this case. Even without the statutory direction,
however, a conclusion that denunciation and deterrence should be the paramount objectives
of sentencing would be inevitable.

[
51
]

It
scarcely needs to be said that rape is an intensely intrusive offence, one that
involves a fundamental violation of the victim’s emotional, psychological and physical
integrity. In the case at bar, a number of circumstances exacerbate the
inherent gravity of the offences.

[
52
]

First
of all, Mr. Katsnelson did not violate the sexual integrity of just one young
woman that morning. After forcing sexual intercourse on C.C. as she lay crying
in her bed, Mr. Katsnelson continued to roam the corridors of the Vanier residence
looking for more victims and eventually raping a second one. The various rooms
that Katsnelson and Connort broke into that morning were the homes of these
young women while they were at university. The victims were asleep in what they
had every right to expect was the safety and security of their bedrooms. The violation
of their privacy was heightened by the fact that both were raped by one
complete stranger while a second one watched. Insofar as C.C. was concerned, it
was also heightened by the fact that Katsnelson took cell phone pictures of
Connort abusing her. The fact that Katsnelson was a stranger to both C.C. and
B.M. is particularly aggravating because it left the victims utterly in the
dark as to the sexual history of their assailant. As Mr. Katsnelson did not use
a condom, they had the perfectly reasonable fear not only of pregnancy but also
of contracting a potentially deadly sexually transmitted disease. Both were
forced to immediately seek medical intervention to reduce the risks that had
been thrust upon them. Further, C.C. suffered a bodily injury that bled for a
week.

[
53
]

In
addition to the physical consequences of the offences for both victims, the
emotional and psychological impact has been profound. It is not possible, at
this point, to know whether the harm that Mr. Katsnelson caused in this respect
is irreparable, but it is clear that as of today, more than 2½ years after the
offences, it has not been repaired.

[
54
]

The
age of the victims is also an aggravating factor. While neither C.C. nor B.M.
were children, neither were they fully adult. As they entered their first week
of university studies in September 2007, away from the protection of their
families, they were standing on the threshold of the rest of their lives.
Tragically, what they encountered was a pair of predators who, I have no doubt,
recognized the vulnerability of young women in that situation and made a
conscious decision to work in concert to exploit it.

[
55
]

It
is significant that the offences were not crimes of opportunity but rather the
product of a premeditated trespass into a university dormitory. Katsnelson and
Connort regarded the teenagers living there as sexual prey. The vulnerability
of the young women whose bedrooms Mr. Katsnelson invaded was not unique to
them. It is shared by thousands of 17 and 18 year olds who leave home every
year to attend colleges and universities across the country. For many,
attending those institutions is a rite of passage along the road from
adolescence to adulthood, and it can be an exciting time. But it can also be a
dangerous time. It is very much in the public interest that college and university
campuses be places of safety and that they be perceived to be places of safety:

R. v. Mai
,
[2001] O.J. No. 1834 (C.A.)
;
R. v. Mizra,

[2006] O.J. No. 1806 (Ont. S.C.)
. Where a court is
confronted with serious offences committed within a university residence by trespassers
like Mr. Katsnelson, a clear and unequivocal response is called for.

(g) The Appropriate Sentence

[
56
]

As I
have said, the paramount objectives of sentencing in this case are the
denunciation and deterrence of the conduct in which Mr. Katsnelson engaged. In
R.
v. C.A.M
.
,
1996 CanLII 230 (SCC)
, [1996] 1 S.C.R. 500, at paragraph
81
, Chief
Justice Lamer stated the following in relation to the function of denunciation:

The objective of denunciation mandates that
a sentence should also communicate society's condemnation of that particular
offender's conduct.  In short, a sentence with a denunciatory element
represents a symbolic, collective statement that the offender's conduct should
be punished for encroaching on our society's basic code of values as enshrined
within our substantive criminal law. As Lord Justice Lawton stated in
R.

v
.
Sargeant

(1974),
60 Cr. App. R. 74
, at p. 77
: "society,
through the courts, must show its abhorrence of particular types of crime, and
the only way in which the courts can show this is by the sentences they
pass".

[
57
]

In
order to determine a fit sentence for Mr. Katsnelson, his conduct on the
morning of September 7, 2007 should be considered in its entirety. The question
to be asked is what sentence, in total, would be proportionate to the gravity
of the whole of his conduct and to his degree of responsibility for it. Approaching
the matter in that way will ensure that the combination of the individual
sentences does not exceed Mr. Katsnelson’s overall culpability. It will also
ensure that sight is not lost of the fact that a central circumstance that
aggravates both the gravity of the offences and Mr. Katsnelson’s degree of
responsibility for them, and that distinguishes this case from all of the
others to which counsel have referred, is the serial nature of the predatory
behaviour on the occasion in question.

[
58
]

When
Mr. Katsnelson’s conduct is considered in this manner, it is clear that the range
of sentence of three to five years proposed by the defence is inadequate. While
the sentence imposed on Justin Connort fell within that range, Connort was in a
significantly different position.  I acknowledge that sentences in the range
suggested by the defence have been imposed for rapes of strangers, even in
cases where the offences occurred after breaking into the victims’ residences. I
also acknowledge that in many of the cases where sentences in excess of five
years have been imposed circumstances were present that are absent from the
case at bar, such as the infliction of extraneous violence, degradation or
threats, or the existence of a prior record. What the present case does have,
however, and what makes it somewhat unique, is a planned and premeditated
targeting of a particularly vulnerable group of young women, leading to
separate rapes of separate victims with the consequent devastation of separate
lives. In my view, the need to give expression to society’s abhorrence of that
conduct and to reflect the extent to which it undermines society’s basic code
of values would not be adequately met by a sentence in the range of three to
five years.

[
59
]

While
denunciation and deterrence are the paramount considerations in determining a
sentence for Mr. Katsnelson, they are not the exclusive considerations. I am
satisfied, for example, that a sentence of imprisonment within the range
suggested by the defence could provide a sufficient measure of specific
deterrence to Mr. Katsnelson. I am also satisfied, for the reasons set forth
earlier, that his rehabilitative prospects are good. He has demonstrated an
ability to make a positive contribution to the community, and he is going to be
returned to the community at some point. I am not persuaded that the ten-year
sentence sought by the Crown gives sufficient weight to Mr. Katsnelson’s prior
positive history and to his potential for rehabilitation. While there is a need
to denounce and deter, there is no need to crush.

III. Disposition

[
60
]

After
giving the matter my best consideration, I am of the view that a fit sentence
for the totality of Mr. Katsnelson’s conduct would be a term of imprisonment of
eight years.

[
61
]

I
would apportion that total as follows. For the offence of sexual assault
causing bodily harm, which carries a greater penalty than sexual assault
simpliciter
,
Mr. Katsnelson is sentenced to five years imprisonment. For the offence of
sexual assault, Mr. Katsnelson is sentenced to a consecutive term of three
years imprisonment.

[
62
]

Thirty
days credit will be subtracted from the three-year sexual assault sentence to
reflect the time spent in custody between the sentencing hearing and today.

[
63
]

There
will be an order under
s. 109(1)
of the
Criminal Code
for life. I
further order that Mr. Katsnelson provide a sample of a bodily substance for
the purpose of forensic DNA analysis, and that he comply with the
Sex
Offender Information Registration Act
for a period of 20 years.
